sections.title: Fan-out, change data capture and CQRS

topics.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous communication

kcs.statement: In synchronous communication the caller blocks until the callee responds, so the caller's latency includes the callee's latency and the call fails when the callee is down.

In asynchronous communication the caller hands work to an intermediary and returns at once, giving up an immediate result in exchange for availability decoupled from the callee and the ability to absorb load spikes.

serves.reason: Deciding which arrows in the diagram go through a queue starts from the sync-vs-async choice

problem_ideas: Checkout calls payment (200 ms), inventory (50 ms) and email (800 ms) synchronously in sequence: compute the user-visible latency, then recompute with email made asynchronous
An order service calls a recommendations service that is down 1% of the time: what fraction of orders fail if the call is synchronous vs queued?
Classify ten operations (login, send welcome email, resize avatar, charge card, update search index…) as must-be-sync or can-be-async and justify each
A user uploads a video and expects a URL immediately: which part is sync and which async?
Failure story: a synchronous chain of five services each at 99.9% uptime; what availability does the caller see?
Interviewer asks 'why not make everything async?': list two costs of asynchrony

lens.reason: Every design interview has a moment where you move slow work off the request path; this is the vocabulary for it.

topics.title: Message queues and load leveling

kcs.statement: A message queue stores messages from producers durably until a consumer acknowledges them, so producers and consumers do not need to be up at the same time.
With competing consumers, each message in a queue is delivered to exactly one of the consumers reading it, so adding consumers increases processing throughput.

With queue-based load leveling, when producers enqueue faster than consumers drain, the backlog grows by the rate difference each second and is worked off after the burst ends, keeping consumer load steady.

serves.reason: Placing a queue in the high-level diagram and justifying it against bursty writes is part of the o4 product

requires.reason: A queue is the intermediary that makes asynchronous communication possible; its purpose cannot be stated without that distinction

problem_ideas: A flash sale enqueues 5,000 orders/s for 2 minutes; 10 workers each process 300/s. Compute the peak backlog and how long until it drains
How many workers are needed to keep the backlog flat at a peak of 12,000 messages/s if each takes 40 ms?
A queue holds 1.2 million messages with 4 KB payloads: how much storage does the backlog need?
Draw where a queue goes in a photo-upload pipeline and name the producer and consumer
A consumer crashes mid-message: what does the queue do with the unacknowledged message?
Interview prompt: 'writes spike 10× at 9 a.m.'—propose a queue and state one trade-off it introduces

lens.reason: Queues appear in almost every interview design; you must be able to size and justify one.

topics.title: Task queues and background jobs

kcs.statement: A task queue holds units of work (such as resizing an image) that workers execute outside the request path, so the API can return 202 Accepted with a job id instead of waiting for the work to finish.
Background jobs are either event-driven (triggered when a message arrives) or schedule-driven (run on a timer such as a nightly cron), and a scheduled job must tolerate running late or twice.

requires.reason: Task queues are message queues whose messages are jobs; workers are competing consumers

problem_ideas: Design the API response and status endpoint for a 3-minute video transcode job

Pick event-driven or schedule-driven for: welcome email, expired-link cleanup, thumbnail generation, monthly invoice

lens.reason: Video processing, notifications and crawlers all rely on workers pulling jobs; interviewers expect you to name them.

topics.title: Back pressure: when the queue keeps growing

kcs.statement: A new message waits roughly backlog size divided by drain rate, so an unbounded queue that keeps growing turns into unbounded latency and eventually memory exhaustion.

Back pressure bounds the queue and pushes the overload back to producers by blocking, slowing or rejecting them (for example HTTP 429 or 503 with Retry-After) instead of accepting work that cannot be finished in time.

requires.reason: Back pressure is defined in terms of queue backlog and drain rate

problem_ideas: Backlog is 600,000 messages and consumers drain 2,000/s: how long does a new message wait?
Your SLA is 5 s from enqueue to processed at 1,000/s drain: what queue bound do you set?
Producers send 3,000/s, consumers drain 2,500/s with 4 GB of memory and 2 KB messages: when does the broker run out?
Compare back pressure with rate limiting: who decides the limit and on what signal?
Failure story: a logging pipeline with an unbounded in-memory buffer takes down the app servers—redesign it
Choose: drop, block or reject for metrics events, payment requests and chat messages

topics.title: Publish/subscribe: one event, many consumers

kcs.statement: In publish/subscribe every subscription on a topic receives its own copy of each message, whereas a point-to-point queue delivers each message to only one consumer.
Publishers do not know their subscribers, so a new downstream service (for example analytics) can subscribe to a topic without any change to the publishing service.

serves.reason: News feed, chat and notification designs all broadcast one event to several services through pub/sub

requires.reason: Pub/sub is taught by contrast with point-to-point queue delivery

problem_ideas: An 'order placed' event must reach billing, shipping, email and analytics: queue or pub/sub, and draw it
A topic has 4 subscriptions and receives 10,000 events/s: how many deliveries per second does the broker make?
Each subscription has 3 competing consumers: how many processes see a given message?
Adding fraud detection to an existing checkout: what changes with pub/sub vs direct calls?
A subscriber is offline for an hour: what happens to its messages with durable vs non-durable subscriptions?
Interviewer: 'how does the notification service learn a new comment was posted?'

lens.reason: The standard way to fan an event out to several services in feed, chat and notification designs.

topics.title: Event streaming, partitions and consumer groups

kcs.statement: An event streaming platform appends events to a retained append-only log and each consumer tracks its own offset, so events are not deleted on consumption and can be replayed from an earlier offset.
Within one consumer group each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so the group's parallelism is capped at the partition count, while every separate consumer group reads all events.
Event streams guarantee order only within a partition, so events that must stay in order (for example all events for one order id) must share a partition key.

requires.reason: Consumer groups are explained as subscriptions that each receive every event
Partitions and partition keys of the log reuse partitioning

problem_ideas: A topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group of 20 consumers: how many are idle?
Events arrive at 60,000/s and one consumer handles 4,000/s: minimum partition count?
A bug corrupted the search index for 6 hours: how does replay from an offset fix it, and what retention is needed?
Ride location updates must stay in order per driver: pick the partition key and name the hot-partition risk
Retention 7 days at 20,000 events/s of 1 KB with replication factor 3: storage needed
Queue or stream: email sending, clickstream analytics, audit log, image resizing

lens.reason: Interviewers often say 'Kafka' expecting you to know partitions, offsets and per-partition ordering.

topics.title: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once

kcs.statement: With at-most-once delivery the consumer acknowledges before processing, so a crash during processing loses the message but never duplicates it.
With at-least-once delivery the consumer acknowledges after processing, so a crash after processing but before the acknowledgement causes redelivery and therefore duplicates.

Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is not achievable in general; systems get exactly-once processing only by combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication that commits atomically with the side effect, or with a destination that itself enforces idempotency.

serves.reason: Naming duplicate delivery as a failure mode and its fix is part of the reliability product

requires.reason: Guarantees are defined by when a consumer acknowledges a queued message

problem_ideas: Trace a timeline: consumer charges a card, crashes before ack—what happens under each guarantee?

topics.title: Idempotency and safe retries

kcs.statement: An operation is idempotent when applying it N times has the same effect as applying it once: 'set balance to 100' is idempotent, 'add 10 to balance' is not.

Retries after a timeout are safe only for idempotent operations, because a timeout does not tell the client whether the server applied the request; by HTTP semantics GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent and POST is not.

serves.reason: Specifying retries as a reliability mechanism requires stating which operations are safe to retry

requires.reason: The idempotency of HTTP methods is a KC here

problem_ideas: Label ten operations idempotent or not: increment like count, set profile photo, append message, delete file, transfer money…
Rewrite 'add 10 credits' so it becomes idempotent
A client times out on POST /orders after 2 s: list the three possible server states
Is DELETE /items/42 returning 404 on the second call still idempotent? Explain
Failure story: a mobile app's automatic retry created duplicate bookings—what was missing?
Turn 'increment view counter' into an idempotent consumer of view events

depth_threads.title: Idempotent but not commutative: ordering still matters

lens.reason: Payment, booking and messaging prompts all turn on whether a retry is safe.

topics.title: Idempotency keys and idempotent consumers

kcs.statement: The client generates a unique idempotency key per logical operation and resends the same key on every retry; the server stores key → result and returns the stored result for a repeat instead of executing again.

The server must record the idempotency key and perform the side effect in the same transaction, otherwise a crash between them re-opens the duplicate window; stored keys expire after a TTL longer than the client's retry horizon.

An idempotent consumer records each processed message id in the same transaction as the message's business effect and skips ids already recorded; when the effect is external (a card charge, an SMS) and cannot share that transaction, local deduplication alone cannot guarantee it happens once, so the external system must enforce idempotency, for example by accepting an idempotency key.

serves.reason: The o5 product explicitly lists an idempotency key as a fix to specify
Payment and booking deep dives in mock interviews expect an idempotency key design

requires.reason: Keys are a mechanism to make non-idempotent operations safe to retry
The idempotent consumer is defined against at-least-once delivery

topics.title: Dead-letter queues and poison messages

kcs.statement: A poison message fails processing every time, so under at-least-once delivery it is redelivered forever, wasting consumer capacity and, in an ordered queue or partition, blocking everything behind it.
After a maximum number of delivery attempts the message is moved to a dead-letter queue, which needs alerting and a redrive path so engineers can inspect, fix and replay the messages.

requires.reason: Endless redelivery of poison messages follows from at-least-once delivery

problem_ideas: A malformed JSON message is at the head of a FIFO queue: describe the system's behaviour with and without a DLQ
Choose max delivery attempts for a payment-webhook consumer vs a thumbnail generator and justify
DLQ receives 50 messages/min after a deploy: what's your runbook?
Distinguish transient failures (database timeout) from permanent ones (schema mismatch): which should hit the DLQ fast?
After fixing a bug you redrive 10,000 DLQ messages: what must the consumer guarantee?
In an event stream partition, how does one poison event stall a whole partition?

topics.title: Short polling vs long polling

kcs.statement: With short polling every T seconds, an update waits T/2 on average to be seen and the server receives clients/T requests per second, most of which return nothing.

With long polling the server holds each request open until data arrives or a timeout fires and the client immediately reissues it, cutting empty responses and delay at the cost of one held connection per waiting client.

requires.reason: Both techniques are patterns of HTTP request/response

problem_ideas: 2M online clients poll every 5 s: compute QPS and the average notification delay
Same clients with long polling at a 30 s timeout and 1 update per client per minute: compute requests per second

topics.title: WebSockets and stateful connection servers

kcs.statement: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with an Upgrade header and then becomes a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection on which both client and server can send frames at any time.

A server holding WebSocket connections is stateful because each connection lives on one server, so the load balancer must support long-lived connections and capacity is planned by concurrent connections per server rather than by QPS.

serves.reason: The chat mock interview requires choosing and scaling WebSockets

requires.reason: WebSockets are motivated and taught by contrast with long polling
The stateful-connection KC is stated against stateless services

topics.title: Server-sent events and choosing a push method

kcs.statement: Server-sent events stream one-way messages from server to client over a single long-lived HTTP response (text/event-stream), and the browser reconnects automatically, resuming with the Last-Event-ID header.

Use server-sent events when only the server pushes (notifications, live scores, streamed tokens), WebSockets when both sides send frequently with low latency (chat, games), and long polling as a fallback where neither is supported.

requires.reason: The selection KC compares SSE against WebSockets

problem_ideas: Pick SSE, WebSockets or long polling for: sports scores, chat, delivery tracking, AI chat token stream, auction bidding
A client on SSE drops for 10 s: how does Last-Event-ID let it catch up, and what must the server retain?

topics.title: Routing messages to millions of open connections

kcs.statement: To deliver a message to user B, the sender's connection server looks up which connection server holds B in a session registry (a key-value store of user → server) and forwards the message there, or publishes it to B's pub/sub channel that B's server subscribes to.
If the recipient has no open connection, the message is persisted for later sync on reconnect and a mobile push notification is sent instead.
Presence (online/last seen) is tracked from connect and disconnect events plus periodic client pings with a timeout, because a dropped connection is not always reported.

serves.reason: The chat system mock requires the cross-server message routing design

requires.reason: Routing is between servers holding WebSocket connections
One routing option is per-user pub/sub channels
The session registry is a key-value store

topics.title: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read

kcs.statement: Fan-out on write pushes each new post id into every follower's precomputed timeline at write time, making reads a single cheap lookup but costing one write per follower.
Fan-out on read assembles a timeline at read time by fetching and merging recent posts from every followed account, making writes cheap but each read cost proportional to the number of followees.
Hybrid fan-out uses fan-out on write for ordinary accounts and fan-out on read for celebrity accounts with millions of followers, merging both at read time to avoid million-write bursts.

serves.reason: The news feed mock interview hinges on this choice

requires.reason: Fan-out on write is performed asynchronously by workers consuming a queue

problem_ideas: 5,000 posts/s with 200 followers on average: timeline writes per second under fan-out on write

topics.title: Change data capture and the outbox pattern

kcs.statement: A dual write (commit to the database, then publish an event) can leave the two out of sync, because a crash or failure between the two steps leaves one done without the other.

Change data capture reads the database's transaction or replication log and emits each committed change as an event, so downstream systems (search index, caches, analytics) follow the database without the application writing twice.

With a transactional outbox the service writes the business row and an event row in the same database transaction, and a relay (often CDC) publishes outbox rows, so an event exists if and only if the change committed.

requires.reason: The outbox depends on atomic transactions
CDC emits changes into an event stream

topics.title: CQRS and event sourcing

kcs.statement: CQRS separates the write model from one or more read models shaped for queries and updated asynchronously from the write side, so read models are eventually consistent with writes.
Event sourcing stores state as an append-only sequence of events and rebuilds current state by replaying them, using periodic snapshots to keep replay time bounded.
CQRS does not require event sourcing, and both add complexity worth paying only when read and write workloads differ greatly in shape or scale, or a full audit history is required.

requires.reason: Read models are materialized views
Read models are fed by an event stream and event sourcing builds on an append-only log

problem_ideas: A bank account has 2M events: with a snapshot every 10,000 events, how many are replayed to load it?
